steps.body:
A critical point is flat. Ask which way it BENDS and the verdict is instant:

**f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) > 0** → flat, bending upward → a **minimum**.
**f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0** → flat, bending downward → a **maximum**.
**f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) = 0** → **inconclusive**. Fall back on the sign chart of f′.

One substitution instead of a whole chart — when it works.

explanationVariants: f′ = 3x² − 12 is zero at x = ±2. f″ = 6x, so f″(2) = 12 > 0 (a minimum) and f″(−2) = −12 < 0 (a maximum).
The sign of f″ at the critical point IS the verdict — no interval testing required.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 12x has f″(x) = 6x. Evaluate f″ at the critical point x = 2.

commonErrors.feedback: That is f″(−2), at the OTHER critical point — where the curve bends downward and there is a maximum.
That is the coefficient. Substitute: f″(2) = 6(2) = 12.
f″ = 6x is zero only at x = 0, which is not a critical point of f at all.

widget.fallbackFeedback: f″(2) = 12 > 0: flat and bending upward, so x = 2 is a minimum.

widget.prompt: Three curves, all with f′(0) = 0 and f″(0) = 0.

panels.title: x⁴
panels.body: f′ = 4x³ and f″ = 12x², so both vanish at 0. And x = 0 is a MINIMUM — the curve is a flat-bottomed bowl.

panels.title: −x⁴
panels.body: Same story: both derivatives vanish at 0. But this one is a MAXIMUM. Identical test results, opposite verdicts.

panels.title: x³
panels.body: Both vanish at 0 again — and this time it is NEITHER, a saddle. Three curves, one test result, three different answers. That is why f″ = 0 is genuinely inconclusive, and why the first-derivative test never stops working.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the third curve is what settles it.
widget.successFeedback: When f″(c) = 0 the test cannot see the difference between a bowl, a dome and a saddle. Only the sign chart of f′ can.

steps.body: That reveal showed the test's blind spot. Now watch it work — on a curve where f″ is nowhere near zero at the points that matter.

predict.prompt: This is f(x) = x³ − 3x. Its tangent goes flat in two places. Do you expect the second-derivative test to return the same verdict at both?

options.label: No — one is a max, the other a min
No — f″ will be 0 at both, like the three curves above

predict.reveal: Drag across both and watch the third pane: f″ = 6x, so it reads −6 at the left flat point and +6 at the right. One test, opposite signs, opposite verdicts.

widget.prompt: Drag to the flat point that the second-derivative test calls a MAXIMUM — the one where the bend is downward.
widget.successFeedback: f′(−1) = 0 and f″(−1) = −6. Flat tangent, bending downward — the test returns MAXIMUM in a single step, and the top pane shows the peak at (−1, 2). That is the whole point: when f″ is not zero it decides immediately. The three curves above were the case where it cannot.
widget.lowFeedback: Not there yet — f′ is still above zero here, so the curve is still climbing toward the peak. The f″ pane is already negative, so the bend is the right one; keep going right until f′ reaches zero.
widget.highFeedback: You have gone past the maximum — come back left. Watch the f″ pane on the way: to the right of x = 0 it is positive, and the flat point over there is the MINIMUM. The test wants the flat point where the bend is downward.

explanationVariants: f″(c) = 0 tells you nothing at all — x⁴ (a minimum), −x⁴ (a maximum) and x³ (a saddle) all produce it. Go back to the sign chart of f′.
The second-derivative test is a shortcut, not a replacement. The first-derivative test always works.

widget.prompt: f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) = 0. What can you conclude?

options.label: Nothing — use the sign chart of f′ instead.
options.feedback: Right. x⁴, −x⁴ and x³ all give this result and are a minimum, a maximum and a saddle respectively.

options.label: It is an inflection point.
options.feedback: It might be — but x⁴ has f″(0) = 0 and is a MINIMUM, with no inflection at all. f″ = 0 needs a sign change to mean anything.

options.label: It is a saddle.
options.feedback: x⁴ has f′(0) = f″(0) = 0 and is a genuine minimum. The test simply cannot see the difference.

options.label: It is a minimum.
options.feedback: −x⁴ has exactly the same test values and is a maximum. The result is inconclusive, which is a real answer and not a failure.

steps.body:
So choose your tool:

**Second-derivative test** — fast, and it works whenever f″(c) ≠ 0. One substitution.
**First-derivative test** — slower, and it NEVER fails. It also handles critical points where f′ does not exist, which f″ cannot even reach.

Try the shortcut. When it shrugs, do the work.

explanationVariants: At a corner, f′ does not exist — so f″ certainly does not either. Only the sign chart of f′ can classify it.
|x| has a minimum at a point where the second-derivative test cannot even be attempted.

widget.prompt: f has a critical point at a CORNER, where f′ does not exist. Which test can classify it?

options.label: The first-derivative test — look at the sign of f′ on either side.
options.feedback: Right. |x| is the standard case: f′ is −1 to the left and +1 to the right, so it is a minimum, and f″ never enters the argument.

options.label: The second-derivative test.
options.feedback: If f′ does not exist at the point, f″ certainly does not. The test cannot even be stated there.

options.label: Neither — corners cannot be classified.
options.feedback: They can, easily: the sign of f′ on either side of the corner tells you everything.

options.label: Both work equally well.
options.feedback: The second-derivative test needs f″(c) to exist, and at a corner it does not.

steps.body: Use the fast tool where it works.
hints: Critical points: 3x(x − 2) = 0, so x = 0 and x = 2.
Evaluate f″ at each: f″(0) = −6 and f″(2) = 6. Which is the MAXIMUM?
explanationVariants: f″(0) = −6 < 0, so x = 0 is a maximum, with f(0) = 4.
The other critical point, x = 2, has f″ = 6 > 0 — a minimum. One substitution each, and both are settled.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 4. Find the local MAXIMUM value of f.

commonErrors.feedback: That is WHERE the maximum occurs. Its VALUE is f(0) = 4.
That is the other critical point, where f″ = 6 > 0 — a minimum, not a maximum.
That is f″(0), which identifies the point as a maximum. Its value is f(0) = 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: f″(0) = −6 < 0 → x = 0 is a maximum, and f(0) = 4.

steps.body: Try the shortcut; keep the workhorse.
takeaways: f′(c) = 0 with f″(c) > 0 is a minimum; with f″(c) < 0, a maximum.
f″(c) = 0 is genuinely inconclusive — x⁴, −x⁴ and x³ all produce it and are all different.
The first-derivative test never fails, and it is the only one that can classify a corner.
steps.teaser: Next: assemble all three charts and draw the curve without plotting a single point.

concept.body: At a flat point, ask which way it bends. Bending UP at a flat point means the flat point is the bottom of a bowl — a minimum. Bending DOWN means it is the top of a dome. And if it is not bending at all, the test has nothing to say.

explanationVariants: f″(c) = −4 < 0 means the curve bends downward at a flat point: the top of a dome, a maximum.
Negative second derivative at a critical point is always a maximum.

widget.prompt: f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) = −4. What is at c?

options.label: A local maximum
options.feedback: Right — flat, and bending downward: the top of a dome.

options.label: A local minimum
options.feedback: That needs f″ > 0 — bending UPWARD at the flat point. Here it bends down.
